summary: Defines Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), a policy-driven protocol between administrative domains for advertising which telephone destinations can be reached and the attributes of routes to them. It works independently of the signaling protocol. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Phone networks need to tell each other which numbers they can reach. This is a way for them to share that information, like cities telling each other which roads lead where.

questions: how do voip domains advertise reachability
what is trip telephony routing over ip
how is trip different from bgp
subtitle: A BGP-style protocol that lets telephony providers advertise which phone numbers they can reach, and by which route.

tldr.problem: Placing an IP telephony call to a phone number in the PSTN means choosing an egress gateway, and that choice depends on the policies and relationships of the providers along the path. A single global directory of gateways is not feasible.
tldr.mechanism: Location servers in different IP Telephony Administrative Domains (ITADs) open TCP peering sessions and exchange UPDATE messages that carry reachable and withdrawn telephone number prefixes plus attributes. Each provider builds its own policy-driven database of routes. TRIP is modeled after BGP-4.
tldr.outcome: TRIP is independent of any signaling protocol, so the same routing protocol can serve SIP and H.323. It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8602.

today: RFC 3219 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2002 and has been updated by RFC 8602. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Telephony Needs Its Own Routing Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 3219 defines the Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) protocol. The RFC calls gateway location and routing one of the more difficult problems in IP telephony. Picking an egress gateway for a call that ends in the PSTN is driven largely by the policies of the parties along the path and the relationships between them.

Because of that, a global directory where users look up destination phone numbers is not a feasible solution. Instead, providers exchange information about egress gateway availability, apply policy, and pass it on. Each provider ends up with its own database of reachable phone numbers and routes, and that database can differ greatly from one provider to the next.

TRIP is an inter-domain protocol. Its speakers are called location servers (LS), and the unit of administration is the IP Telephony Administrative Domain (ITAD): the set of gateways, location servers and other resources under one administrative authority. TRIP is modeled after BGP-4, with some link-state ideas borrowed from OSPF, IS-IS and the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (SCSP).

TRIP runs over a reliable transport, so it needs no fragmentation, retransmission, acknowledgment or sequencing of its own. It is independent of the signaling protocol, so it can serve both H.323 and SIP. It does not define a route selection algorithm.
sections.eli5: Imagine every phone company has a different list of which numbers it can call and who helps along the way. Instead of one giant phone book for everybody, each company swaps notes with its neighbors and keeps its own list.

sections.title: Routes, Peers and the Routing Databases
sections.content:
In TRIP, a route is a set of destination addresses (an address family plus an address prefix) combined with an application protocol such as SIP or H.323. A route covers a range of numbers by being a prefix of them. Arbitrary ranges are expressed by listing several prefixes.

Two location servers that share a transport connection are peers. Peers in the same ITAD are internal peers; otherwise they are external peers. Externally, TRIP uses point-to-point peering. Inside an ITAD, it floods updates over any connected topology, so unlike BGP it does not require a full mesh of internal peers.

Each location server keeps a Telephony Routing Information Base (TRIB) made of four parts:

  • Adj-TRIBs-In: unprocessed routes learned from each peer, kept separately per peer.
  • Ext-TRIB: the best external and local routes, one per LS.
  • Loc-TRIB: routes selected by applying local policy to the internal Adj-TRIBs-In and the Ext-TRIB.
  • Adj-TRIBs-Out: routes chosen for advertisement to external peers.

This is a conceptual model. An implementation does not need four separate copies of the data.

After a session is established the first data flow is a dump of the relevant routes, and later only incremental updates are sent. TRIP does not require periodic refresh, so a location server must retain the current version of every routing entry. A route can be withdrawn by listing it in WithdrawnRoutes, by advertising a replacement with the same destinations, or, for external peers, by closing the peer connection.

Aggregation combines several routes into one less specific route to reduce the size of the TRIB. It is optional and decided by local policy. When the aggregated routes do not share a next hop, the aggregate's NextHopServer must be a signaling server in the aggregating LS's own domain.
sections.eli5: Each location server keeps four piles of papers: what neighbors told it, what it chose to believe, what it uses itself, and what it plans to tell others. Squishing many small notes into one bigger note saves space.

sections.title: The Four TRIP Messages
sections.content:
Messages travel over a reliable transport. A message must be processed only after it is entirely received. The maximum message size is 4096 octets, and all implementations must support it. The smallest message is the 3-octet header with no data.

Every message starts with a header holding a 2-octet Length (the total length including the header, at least 3 and at most 4096, with no padding allowed) and a 1-octet Type. Four types exist: OPEN, UPDATE, NOTIFICATION and KEEPALIVE.

OPEN is the first message each side sends after the transport connection comes up. It is at least 17 octets and carries the version (currently 1), a proposed Hold Time, the sender's ITAD number, a 4-octet TRIP Identifier that must uniquely identify the LS within its ITAD, and optional parameters. The negotiated Hold Time is the smaller of the two proposals and must be zero or at least three seconds. The one defined optional parameter is Capability Information, which carries Route Types Supported and Send Receive Capability.

UPDATE carries a list of attributes and can advertise and withdraw routes at the same time. It has no mandatory attributes, though some are conditionally mandatory. Attributes must appear in increasing order of type code and at most once.

KEEPALIVE is just the 3-octet header. It is sent often enough that the Hold Timer does not expire, with one third of the Hold Time suggested as a reasonable maximum interval, and never more than once every 3 seconds. If the negotiated Hold Time is zero, periodic keepalives must not be sent.

NOTIFICATION reports an error and the connection is closed right after it. It holds a 1-octet error code, a 1-octet subcode and diagnostic data. The codes are Message Header Error, OPEN Message Error, UPDATE Message Error, Hold Timer Expired, Finite State Machine Error and Cease.
sections.eli5: There are only four kinds of notes: hello, news, still-here, and something-went-wrong. Each note begins with a tiny label saying how long it is and which kind it is.

sections.title: TRIP Attributes
sections.content:
An UPDATE is a sequence of attributes, each with a flags octet, a type code octet and a 2-octet length. The flags say how to treat an attribute the receiver does not recognize: well-known or not, transitive or not, dependent or independent, partial, and whether link-state encapsulation is used. An LS that passes along an unrecognized transitive attribute must set the Partial flag.

The three base attributes are WithdrawnRoutes, ReachableRoutes and ITAD Topology. Routes inside them have an address family (1 Decimal Routing Numbers, 2 PentaDecimal Routing Numbers, 3 E.164 Numbers), an application protocol (1 SIP, 2 H.323-H.225.0-Q.931, 3 H.323-H.225.0-RAS, 4 H.323-H.225.0-Annex-G), a length, and an address prefix written as ASCII digits. The E.164 family should be used whenever possible.

The other attributes shape routing decisions:

  • NextHopServer names the server, as a domain name or IP address with optional port, to which signaling should be sent. The default port is assumed when none is given, for example 5060 for SIP.
  • AdvertisementPath records the ITADs an advertisement passed through, like AS_PATH in BGP. A route whose path already contains the local ITAD must be discarded, which prevents loops.
  • RoutedPath records the ITADs that signaling messages would actually traverse. It changes only when the next hop changes.
  • AtomicAggregate and ConvertedRoute are zero-length flags. The first marks a less specific route chosen over a more specific one. The second must be added when an LS changes a route's application protocol.
  • LocalPreference is used only inside a domain and MultiExitDisc expresses a preferred link between two domains.
  • Communities groups destinations. The well-known NO_EXPORT community means a route must not be advertised outside the receiving ITAD.

The ITAD Topology attribute lists the internal peers of an LS. It lets the other servers in a domain detect a failed LS and purge the routes it originated. It must never be sent to an inter-domain peer.
sections.eli5: Each route comes with sticky notes: where to send the call next, which towns the news passed through, and how much you like this route. Some notes are only for people in your own town.

sections.title: Peering Sessions and the State Machine
sections.content:
TRIP runs over TCP and uses port 6069. Each peer has its own finite state machine, borrowed from BGP, with six states: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm and Established. A session starts in Idle. After a Start event the LS begins connecting and listening, and moves to Connect.

Once the transport is up, each side sends an OPEN. If the received OPEN is fine, it replies with a KEEPALIVE and moves to OpenConfirm. Receiving a KEEPALIVE there moves it to Established, where UPDATE, KEEPALIVE and NOTIFICATION messages flow. If the ITAD number in the peer's OPEN equals the local one, the connection is internal; otherwise it is external.

When both sides try to connect at once, the connection initiated by the LS with the higher TRIP Identifier is kept. A collision with a connection already in the Established state always closes the new connection.

After an error the machine returns to Idle. To avoid flapping, automatic Start events must not be generated immediately, and the delay must grow exponentially, with an initial value of 60 seconds suggested. Peers may also negotiate the protocol version by retrying with lower versions after an Unsupported Version Number error.

Capability negotiation lets a peer declare a mode. In Send Only mode a server only sends updates, in Receive Only mode it only listens (useful for management stations), and the default is Send Receive. Two peers cannot both be Send Only or both Receive Only, and such a mismatch ends in a NOTIFICATION with the Capability Mismatch subcode.
sections.eli5: Two servers shake hands in steps: knock, say hello, confirm the hello, then chat. If anything goes wrong they hang up and wait a bit longer each time before trying again.

sections.title: Flooding and the Decision Process
sections.content:
An UPDATE may only be processed in the Established state, after the error checks pass. Withdrawn routes are removed from the matching Adj-TRIB-In, and new routes are placed there. The LS then reruns its Decision Process whenever a change makes an earlier route unavailable or adds new destinations.

Inside a domain, updates are synchronized by flooding. Link-state encapsulated attributes carry the originator's TRIP Identifier and a sequence number. A route is new if it is not yet stored or has a greater sequence number. New routes are forwarded to all other internal peers, while old ones are ignored. Withdrawn routes are kept marked as withdrawn for MaxPurgeTime seconds. Sequence numbers run from 1 to 2^31-1, and an LS that restarts begins again at the minimum value.

The Decision Process has three phases. Phase 1 computes a degree of preference for each route: from the LocalPreference attribute if it came from an internal peer, or from configured policy if it came from an external one. Phase 2 picks the best route per destination and installs it in the Loc-TRIB. Phase 3 disseminates routes to external peers and may aggregate them. All internal LSs in a domain must apply the same decision criteria, otherwise their Loc-TRIBs cannot be synchronized.

The RFC gives only two fixed route selection rules: a route with the local ITAD in its AdvertisementPath cannot be better than any other, and an ITAD must avoid unstable routes and rapid spontaneous changes.
sections.eli5: When one server in a town hears news, it tells every other server in town, and each ticket has a number so nobody acts on old news. Then each server picks its favorite route for every number.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
RFC 3219 creates a new IANA registry for TRIP parameters: capabilities, attributes, address families, application protocols and ITAD numbers. The value 0 is reserved in each so that an unset parameter is distinguishable from a real one.

The high ranges are for private or vendor-specific use: capability codes 32768 to 65535, attribute type codes 224 to 255, and address family and application protocol codes 32768 to 65535. New capabilities need a specification, and new attribute codes in the range 12 to 223 need a specification that covers the points in section 5.12 of the RFC. New address families and application protocols are subject to Expert Review.

ITAD numbers 1 to 255 are for private use. Numbers from 256 to (2**32)-1 are allocated by IANA on a first-come, first-served basis, and a request must describe the organization that will administer the ITAD and give contact information.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of the codes TRIP uses, so that two companies never use the same number for different things. Some numbers are saved for private use.

sections.title: Securing Peer Sessions
sections.content:
The RFC states that a security mechanism is clearly needed to stop unauthorized entities from setting up peer sessions with location servers or interfering with authorized ones. For TRIP over TCP in an IP network, that mechanism is IPsec, using either the Authentication Header or Encapsulating Security Payload.

AH gives data origin authentication, connectionless integrity and optional anti-replay protection. ESP adds confidentiality. Implementations that use either header must comply with the minimum algorithm sets defined for them. Implementations SHOULD use IKE for more robust keying, and those that do SHOULD support authentication with RSA signatures and RSA public key encryption.

A transport mode security association between two hosts is the form appropriate for protecting a session between two peer LSs.
sections.eli5: If anyone could join the note-passing, they could send fake directions. So the servers lock their notes with IPsec and check who they are talking to.
